title: How to park threads in cross-stitch
subtitle: Leaving a colour in place while working an adjacent colour
excerpt: Parking threads means leaving a threaded needle waiting in the fabric rather than ending and re-starting the thread each time you switch colours. The parked needle rests at the point where the colour will next be needed, so you pick it up and continue without searching or counting from scratch.
sourceNotes: The parking technique is a widely documented efficiency method in cross-stitch. The stitch-by-stitch and column-by-column variations described here follow established convention.

glossaryTerms.definition: Leaving a threaded needle inserted in the fabric at the point where the colour will next be needed, rather than ending and re-starting the thread each time a colour is temporarily set aside.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

content.text: a thread means pushing the needle (still threaded) into the fabric at the next square where that colour appears, then setting it aside while you stitch with another colour. When you reach that square, pick up the waiting needle and carry on without ending the thread or counting from the chart.

Parking is most useful on projects with many closely spaced colours that each appear in small isolated groups across a wide area. The technique lets you work a whole column or row section by section across all the colours at once, rather than finishing one colour completely before starting the next. The trade-off is that you will have many needles in the fabric at once, which takes some getting used to.
Work the last full cross of the current colour that you can reach without having to jump more than one or two squares.
Insert the threaded needle from the back through the starting hole of the next same-colour square on the chart. That is the bottom-left hole of that square.
Leave the needle and its thread resting on the fabric surface. Do not pull it through.
Pick up the next colour's needle and work the stitches for that colour in this area. Lay its needle aside in the same way when you finish.
When you reach the parked colour's square, pick up that needle, pull the
through to the front, and continue stitching.

items.symptom: The parked threads tangle on the front of the fabric
items.cause: Too many needles parked close together with no organisation, or the needles are long enough to cross over each other.
items.fix: Park each needle only as far from the last stitch as necessary. Use shorter needles (size 26 instead of 24) so there is less thread dangling.

items.symptom: A parked needle has come loose and the thread slipped back through the fabric
items.cause: The needle was parked in a hole that is too loose for the thread count.
items.fix: When parking on fine Aida, angle the needle slightly so it grips the weave. On very fine fabric, push the needle further through the fabric so it holds itself horizontally against the surface.

content.text: The parking technique is most rewarding on a project with many colours spread across a small area, such as a portrait or a complex floral arrangement. Try it on the next project that has five or more colours appearing in adjacent squares.
